claim: DENV causes approximately 390 million infections annually
source: DENV alone causes approximately 390 million infections and 10,000 deaths annually (Bhatt et al., 2013; Messina et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhatt et al., 2013 and Messina et al., 2019

claim: DENV causes approximately 10,000 deaths annually
source: DENV alone causes approximately 390 million infections and 10,000 deaths annually (Bhatt et al., 2013; Messina et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhatt et al., 2013 and Messina et al., 2019

claim: Half of the world's population is exposed to arboviral vectors
source: Arthropod-borne viruses, or arboviruses, such as Dengue (DENV), Zika (ZIKV), and Chikungunya (CHIKV), are a significant cause of disease globally, with half of the world's population exposed to arboviral vectors.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the introduction

claim: Arboviruses must cycle between vertebrate and invertebrate hosts
source: Arboviruses must cycle between vertebrate and invertebrate hosts, which differ significantly in body temperature, cellular environment, and mode of antiviral immunity, raising questions about the evolutionary strategies they may employ to replicate in these different host environments.
evidence: Stated as established biological fact

claim: Vertebrate and invertebrate hosts differ significantly in body temperature, cellular environment, and mode of antiviral immunity
source: Arboviruses must cycle between vertebrate and invertebrate hosts, which differ significantly in body temperature, cellular environment, and mode of antiviral immunity, raising questions about the evolutionary strategies they may employ to replicate in these different host environments.
evidence: Stated as established biological knowledge

claim: RNA viruses exist as a dynamic population of co-circulating genotypes surrounding a master sequence
source: RNA viruses exist as a dynamic population of co-circulating genotypes surrounding a master sequence (Domingo, 2002; Domingo et al., 2012; Holland et al., 1992; Lauring and Andino, 2010; Wilke, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: The distribution and dynamics of minor alleles play important roles in population fitness, adaptation, and disease
source: It is becoming increasingly clear that the distribution and dynamics of minor alleles play important roles in population fitness, adaptation, and disease (Andino and Domingo, 2015; Bordería et al., 2015; Grad et al., 2014; Shirogane et al., 2012; Vignuzzi et al., 2006; Xue et al., 2018, Xue et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: CirSeq can detect alleles as rare as 1 in 10^6 in frequency
source: Recently, high-accuracy sequencing approaches that control for sequencing errors through barcoding, like PrimerID (Jabara et al., 2011), or through template circularization and amplification, like Circular Sequencing (CirSeq) (Acevedo et al., 2014; Acevedo and Andino, 2014), can detect alleles as rare as 1 in 106 in frequency.
evidence: Supported by citations to CirSeq methodology papers

claim: DENV was serially passaged in human and mosquito cell lines for nine passages
source: Starting from infectious vRNA transcribed from a plasmid encoding dengue virus type 2 (DENV Type 2, Thailand/16681/84), we serially passaged viral populations in two well characterized cell lines used for DENV research: the human hepatoma-derived cell line Huh7 or the Aedes albopictus-derived cell line C6/36, for nine passages.
evidence: Described as experimental procedure performed in this study

claim: Each passage infected 5 × 10^6 cells at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1
source: To control the influence of drift due to genetic bottlenecks and recombination and complementation between viral variants (Clarke et al., 1993; Wahl et al., 2002), each passage infected 5 × 106 cells at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1, using a viral inoculum of 5 × 105 focus forming units (FFU) from the previous passage.
evidence: Described as experimental procedure performed in this study

claim: The virus undergoes 1–3 rounds of replication in each passage
source: We estimate the virus undergoes 1–3 rounds of replication in each passage.
evidence: Estimated from experimental conditions

claim: Adapted populations show increased virus production on their adapted hosts
source: Viral production assays comparing mosquito-adapted (top panel) and human-adapted (bottom panel) DENV populations. Adapted populations show increased virus production on their adapted hosts.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1c with experimental data

claim: Cellular DENV RNA is significantly decreased when adapted lines are propagated on the by-passed, alternative host
source: Analysis of viral RNA content by qRT-PCR. Cellular DENV RNA is significantly decreased when adapted lines are propagated on the by-passed, alternative host.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1d with qRT-PCR data

claim: Focus size increased markedly throughout passage on the adapted host
source: Focus forming assays of the adapted lineages performed on each population over the course of passage. Passages 1, 5, and 9 are shown for all lineages. Focus size increased markedly throughout passage on the adapted host.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1e with focus forming assay data

claim: Passaging on one host cell line was accompanied by a concurrent loss of fitness in the alternative host cell line
source: In agreement with previous studies (Byk and Gamarnik, 2016; Greene et al., 2005; Johnson et al., 1994; Novella et al., 1995; Vasilakis et al., 2009; Villordo et al., 2015; Villordo and Gamarnik, 2013), passaging on one host cell line was accompanied by a concurrent loss of fitness in the alternative host cell line (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1c and citations to previous studies

claim: Human-adapted virus showed a uniform small focus phenotype when plated on mosquito cells
source: For instance, the human-adapted virus showed a uniform small focus phenotype when plated on mosquito cells (Figure 1f).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1f with focus forming assay images

claim: Mosquito-adapted populations formed fewer foci in human cells
source: In contrast, mosquito-adapted populations formed fewer foci in human cells (Figure 1f).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1f with focus forming assay images

claim: Mosquito-adapted populations exhibited a heterogeneous focus phenotype, with small and large foci
source: Mosquito-adapted populations exhibited a heterogeneous focus phenotype, with small and large foci, suggesting they contain distinct variants which differentially affect replication in human cells.
evidence: Observed in experimental data and interpreted

claim: Similar EOPs were observed for all primate-derived cells
source: Similar EOPs were observed for all primate-derived cells, indicating the adaptation and de-adaptation observed upon passage in either Huh7 or C6/36 cells largely reflect changes in fitness to the mammalian vs insect cell environments and distinct cellular machineries.
evidence: Based on experimental EOP measurements across cell lines

claim: C6/36 cells exhibit altered RNA-mediated antiviral immunity
source: For instance, C6/36 cells exhibit altered RNA-mediated antiviral immunity (Brackney et al., 2010; Scott et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Huh7.5.1 cells are RIG-I-deficient
source: Huh7.5.1 cells are RIG-I-deficient (Shirasago et al., 2015; Zhong et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Vero cells are deficient in type-I interferon production
source: Vero cells are deficient in type-I interferon production (Saito et al., 2020; Desmyter et al., 1968; Osada et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: CirSeq yielded an average of approximately 2 × 10^5−2 × 10^6 reads per base across the genome for each viral population
source: With an error rate of less than 1 in 106, CirSeq yielded an average of approximately 2 × 105−2 × 106 reads per base across the genome for each viral population in our experiments (Figure 2a; Acevedo et al., 2014; Whitfield and Andino, 2016).
evidence: Reported from sequencing data analysis

claim: CirSeq has an error rate of less than 1 in 10^6
source: With an error rate of less than 1 in 106, CirSeq yielded an average of approximately 2 × 105−2 × 106 reads per base across the genome for each viral population in our experiments (Figure 2a; Acevedo et al., 2014; Whitfield and Andino, 2016).

claim: CirSeq permits the accurate quantification of alleles as rare as 1 in 60,000–600,000 genomes

claim: Most alleles are present at low frequencies, between 1 in 1000 and 1 in 100,000

source: However, many alleles rapidly increased in frequency with passage number (Video 1).

claim: Cell-adaptation increased the frequency of alleles in specific regions of the DENV genome, such as NS2A and NS4B in human-adapted lineages

claim: Cell-adaptation increased the frequency of alleles in E, NS3, and the 3′ UTR in mosquito-adapted replicates

claim: The first two PCA components partitioned the viral lineages along two orthogonal, host-specific paths
source: The first two components, which explain 83% of the observed variance (Figure 2d left panel and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c), partitioned the viral lineages along two orthogonal, host-specific paths, radiating outward in order of passage number from the original WT genotype (Figure 2d, left panel).
evidence: Shown in PCA analysis in Figure 2d

claim: The third and fourth PCA components explained 13.4% of the observed variance
source: The third and fourth components in the PCA explained 13.4% of the observed variance and further partitioned each lineage along orthogonal, replicate-specific axes (Figure 2d right panel for human series A and B and mosquito series A and B).

claim: The 3′ UTR and E contained the strongest signatures of mosquito-specific adaptation
source: The 3′ UTR and E contained the strongest signatures of mosquito-specific adaptation.

claim: Human-specific alleles were distributed across the genome, including nonsynonymous substitutions in E, NS2A, and NS4B
source: Human-specific alleles were distributed across the genome, including nonsynonymous substitutions in E, NS2A, and NS4B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).

claim: MDS revealed the orthogonal, host-specific evolutionary paths of the populations
source: MDS also revealed the orthogonal, host-specific evolutionary paths of the populations (Figure 2e).

claim: C-to-U mutations occurred at the highest rate, approximately 5 × 10^−4 s/n/r in all populations

claim: The genomic mutation rate was 0.70 and 0.73 s/g/r for mosquito populations
source: The genomic mutation rate, substitutions per genome per replication (s/g/r) (⎧g), was calculated by taking the sum of the ML mutation rate estimates of all single-nucleotide mutations across the genome, yielding ⎧g estimates of 0.70 and 0.73 s/g/r for mosquito populations
evidence: Calculated from mutation rate data in Supplementary file 2

claim: The genomic mutation rate was 0.61 and 0.60 s/g/r for human populations
source: The genomic mutation rate, substitutions per genome per replication (s/g/r) (⎧g), was calculated by taking the sum of the ML mutation rate estimates of all single-nucleotide mutations across the genome, yielding ⎧g estimates of 0.70 and 0.73 s/g/r for mosquito populations and 0.61 and 0.60 s/g/r for human populations (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Calculated from mutation rate data in Supplementary file 2

claim: The virus has a probability of acquiring less than one mutation per genome per replication cycle
source: These estimates, indicating that the virus has a probability of acquiring less than one mutation per genome per replication cycle (Figure 3f), are consistent with genomic mutation rate estimates for other positive-strand RNA viruses (Drake and Holland, 1999).
evidence: Inferred from genomic mutation rate estimates and compared to literature

claim: 8–12% of variants are lethal
source: Based on these classifications, we assessed the total proportion of mutations in each class, finding 8–12% of variants are lethal, 25–28% significantly deleterious, and only 0.5–1.5% significantly beneficial (Figure 3e).
evidence: Calculated from fitness classifications shown in Figure 3e

claim: 25–28% of variants are significantly deleterious
source: Based on these classifications, we assessed the total proportion of mutations in each class, finding 8–12% of variants are lethal, 25–28% significantly deleterious, and only 0.5–1.5% significantly beneficial (Figure 3e).
evidence: Calculated from fitness classifications shown in Figure 3e

claim: Only 0.5–1.5% of variants are significantly beneficial
source: Based on these classifications, we assessed the total proportion of mutations in each class, finding 8–12% of variants are lethal, 25–28% significantly deleterious, and only 0.5–1.5% significantly beneficial (Figure 3e).
evidence: Calculated from fitness classifications shown in Figure 3e

claim: DENV genomes have a 40–50% probability to acquire a deleterious mutation per replication cycle
source: We estimate DENV genomes have a 40–50% probability to acquire a deleterious mutation but only a 0.2–0.3% probability to acquire a beneficial mutation per replication cycle (Figure 3f).

claim: DENV genomes have only a 0.2–0.3% probability to acquire a beneficial mutation per replication cycle
source: We estimate DENV genomes have a 40–50% probability to acquire a deleterious mutation but only a 0.2–0.3% probability to acquire a beneficial mutation per replication cycle (Figure 3f).
evidence: Calculated from fitness class-specific mutation rates shown in Figure 3f

claim: Non-structural proteins were significantly enriched in deleterious and lethal mutations compared to structural proteins
source: Non-structural proteins were significantly enriched in deleterious and lethal mutations compared to structural proteins.

claim: DENV structural proteins exhibit higher mutational robustness compared to non-structural proteins
source: This finding contrasts with results obtained from analyses of poliovirus population dynamics (Acevedo et al., 2014). Whereas DENV structural proteins exhibit higher mutational robustness compared to non-structural proteins, poliovirus structural proteins were found to be less robust to mutation than nonstructural proteins (Acevedo et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of fitness effects and contrasted with poliovirus data

claim: In Influenza A, membrane-associated HA and NA proteins were more robust to mutation than 'internal' proteins
source: Interestingly, in a mutational screening study in Influenza A, another enveloped virus, membrane-associated HA and NA proteins were more robust to mutation than 'internal' proteins (Visher et al., 2016).

claim: The viral UTRs exhibit host-specific patterns of constraint

claim: In human cells, the DENV UTRs were more brittle but also contained more beneficial alleles than in mosquito adapted populations
source: In human cells, the DENV UTRs were more brittle but also contained more beneficial alleles than in mosquito adapted populations, suggesting strong selection.

claim: Deleterious and lethal mutations exhibited significant overlap between the two hosts

claim: Viral protein and RNA structures and functions share common constraints in the two host environments
source: This indicates viral protein and RNA structures and functions share common constraints in the two host environments.

claim: Synonymous mutations tended to be more neutral than non-synonymous mutations

claim: Non-conservative changes exhibited significantly greater deleterious fitness effects than conservative changes
source: Non-conservative changes exhibited significantly greater deleterious fitness effects than conservative changes, emphasizing the impact of biophysical properties on fitness effects as well as the sensitivity of our approach to uncover these differences (Pechmann and Frydman, 2014).

claim: Lethal alleles were enriched in nonsense mutations
source: As expected, lethal alleles were enriched in nonsense mutations (Figure 3j, 'Stop') as well as nonsynonymous substitutions (Figure 3j).

claim: In early passages, the population is dominated by neutral and deleterious alleles that arise continuously in each replication cycle

claim: In later passages, rare beneficial mutations begin to accumulate under positive selection

claim: The deleterious genetic load is never fully purged from the viral populations
source: However, because most mutations arising during replication are deleterious or neutral (Figure 3f), the deleterious genetic load is never fully purged from the viral populations.

claim: Mean fitness of the population is less than 1.0 early in passage

claim: Lethal mutations exert minimal effect on the population because they are rapidly purged and remain only at very low frequencies

source: We find that adaptive mutations, including changes in coding and noncoding regions, cluster in specific regions across the DENV genome.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5a mapping fitness effects across genome

claim: Mutations in clusters can lead to similar phenotypic outcomes
source: Examination of mosquito specific alterations in a glycosylation site in protein E and in the 3′ UTR suggest that mutations in these clusters can lead to similar phenotypic outcomes.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5c-e for E protein and Figure 5h-i for 3' UTR

claim: The process of alternating host adaptation relies on maintaining access adaptive phenotypes through highly connected genetic networks made up of phenotypically redundant mutations
source: This suggests that the process of alternating host adaptation relies on maintaining access adaptive phenotypes through highly connected genetic networks made up of phenotypically redundant mutations.
evidence: Inferred from observation of phenotypically equivalent mutations

claim: The phenotypic redundancy of mutations increases the mutational target size associated with key transitions necessary for adaptation
source: We propose that the phenotypic redundancy of such mutations increases the mutational target size associated with key transitions necessary for adaptation, thereby partially relieving possible bottlenecks associated with transmission and early adaptation (Besnard et al., 2020; Girgis et al., 2012).
evidence: Proposed based on observations and supported by citations

claim: Adaptive mutations are largely excluded from transmembrane domains and structured regions in DENV proteins
source: Adaptive mutations are largely excluded from transmembrane domains and structured regions in DENV proteins.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6a-b analyzing enrichment by biophysical properties

claim: The sequence of arboviral transmembrane and structured domains is poised at a compromise that optimizes function in the distinct environments of human and mosquito cells
source: It is tempting to speculate that the sequence of these arboviral domains is poised at a compromise that optimizes function in the distinct environments of human and mosquito cells (Bourg et al., 2019; Shoval et al., 2012; Tendler et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculated based on observations and supported by citations

claim: The relaxed structural constraints of IDRs allow them to explore more mutational diversity without compromising protein folding or stability
source: The relaxed structural constraints of IDRs allow them to explore more mutational diversity without compromising protein folding or stability, thus enabling access to more extensive sets of adaptive mutations (Charon et al., 2018; Gitlin et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from enrichment data and supported by citations

claim: Viral IDRs may rewire viral protein interactions with host factors, thereby driving adaptation to changing environments
source: Such plasticity may allow viral IDRs to rewire viral protein interactions with host factors, thereby driving adaptation to changing environments (Figure 6f).
evidence: Speculated based on IDR properties

claim: The link between structural properties and fitness effects measured in our study mirrors sequence conservation and variation across natural isolates of DENV and ZIKV
source: Notably, the link between structural properties and fitness effects measured in our study mirrors sequence conservation and variation across natural isolates of DENV and ZIKV (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6c-d comparing fitness classes to conservation

claim: The relationships between adaptability, structural flexibility, and phenotypic redundancy uncovered here can suggest general principles of flavivirus evolution broadly
source: This indicates that the relationships between adaptability, structural flexibility, and phenotypic redundancy uncovered here in a model of DENV adaptation to cultured human and mosquito cells can suggest general principles of flavivirus evolution broadly.
evidence: Inferred from agreement between short-term and long-term evolution patterns

claim: Ae. albopictus is increasingly understood to be an urban vector species in DENV transmission
source: Although Ae. aegypti is the primary mosquito vector of DENV, Ae. albopictus is increasingly understood to be an urban vector species in DENV transmission (Kamgang et al., 2019; Lambrechts et al., 2010; Moncayo et al., 2004; Rezza, 2012).
evidence: Cited from multiple references

claim: DENV2 clone 16681 was isolated from a patient in Bangkok, Thailand in 1964
source: DENV-2 clone 16681 was isolated from a patient in Bangkok, Thailand in 1964 (Kinney et al., 1997)
evidence: Cited from Kinney et al., 1997
